# Independent audit: shaking a tetrahedron into a square pyramid

Audited `candidate eba4cea978b206ae` in full. The exact counterexample passes.

The four tetrahedron inequalities give precisely the stated vertical chords, including the full square projection. Their length is 2(1-max(|x_1|,|x_2|)), so the one-sided shake is the square pyramid of volume 8/3. The opposite shake is its reflection. The barycentric-coordinate cap bound gives maximum tetrahedron depth at most 27/64 for every candidate point.

For the height-one pyramid, the representation (RU,RV,1-R) with density 3r^2 is the correct normalized volume law. Conditioning an upward through-Y cut on Z=aU+bV gives the stated threshold R<=h/(1-Z), with saturation exactly at Z=1-h. Symmetrization therefore gives the displayed g. Its elementary lower bound h^3 exceeds 7/16 by the exact positive amount 369/250000.

I recomputed both branches of I(A). The antiderivative on the first branch is h^3 A/(1-A^2)^2; matching at A=1-h gives the second branch exactly. The claimed upper bound 9/16 reduces to the polynomial F shown in the note. Dropping its nonnegative cubic and minimizing the remaining quadratic yields 2484/15625-961/8800=273743/5500000>0. Thus this step is a global exact bound, not a numerical check of finitely many slopes.

The density of |aU+bV| is nonincreasing for every pair of real coefficients, after absorbing their signs by symmetry. Its trapezoidal/triangular/uniform cases are all mixtures of uniform interval densities with the stated Stieltjes weights. Consequently the uniform-average bound applies to EVERY upward orientation. Taking complementary sides then gives the lower bound 7/16 for EVERY downward orientation, and zero vertical coefficient gives exactly one half. Boundaries are null under the continuous volume, and translating a containing halfspace boundary to Y gives a smaller containing cap. This completes the all-halfspace certificate.

The binary product identity has the correct exact factor 2^(-n): own-fiber restriction supplies the lower bound, while a finite exposing base tilt excludes all other fibers without altering the chosen continuous cut. All fiber volumes remain unchanged under the shake.

The final edge-direction qualification is also correct. When a tetrahedron is projected parallel to one of its edges, that edge projects to one vertex of a triangle and the other two vertices project to the other two projection vertices. The lower endpoint of every chord is affine over this triangle, as is its chord length. Subtracting the lower affine endpoint is an affine shear, so the edge-parallel shake is another affine-equivalent tetrahedron. Adding this one-sentence explanation to the source would make its last qualification self-contained, but it is not needed for the counterexample.

No correction to the counterexample or constants is needed. It rules out both choices of one-sided shaking along an arbitrary prescribed axis; it does not rule out an additional theorem choosing a different axis from the body.
